checklist.fact: The City of Federal Way (WA) is the issuer, seeking proposals from experienced, qualified Vendors that can provide ERP software and services meeting all of the City's functional and technical requirements.
The City intends to purchase an integrated ERP solution and to implement it as a replacement ERP, using a phased approach or one recommended by the selected Vendor and approved by the City.
The City will also accept responses from vendors offering best-of-breed Human Capital Management solutions, which must be able to integrate with the selected ERP system.
Proposals are due September 17, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, and late submissions will not be considered.
Vendor questions are due August 28, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, with the RFP issued August 16, 2024.
The estimated timeline has implementation running from March 2025 to January 2027, after finalist selection in October 2024, demos in December 2024, and due diligence in January 2025.

Proposals are scored on Software (30), Technology (15), Vendor (15), Cost Value (15) and Implementation (25), and the Implementation criterion requires Go Live for all modules in scope by January 1, 2027.
Pricing must be comprehensive (including all taxes and discounts), valid for 180 days, and cover software, implementation services, and license/maintenance for Years 1-10.
Proposals must be emailed as one PDF of no more than 100 pages (excluding sample contracts) plus the Requirements document in MS Word format.
The pricing basis is 130 named users and 85 concurrent users for Financials, and 400 FTEs and 744 W2s for Human Capital Management.

The detailed modules and functionality are defined in a separate Requirements Word document that is not included in this PDF; vendors must rate each item, and missing many Required features may lead to elimination.

The new ERP replaces Eden (financials, HR, time and attendance, payroll), Quadrant cashiering and Excel-based budget and ACFR, and must integrate with retained systems such as NeoGov, Power Time, Amanda and RecTrac.

component_records.title: Bid administration and clarification management
component_records.description: Manages the solicitation process itself: compiles the bid team's questions on the RFP, its attachments and the separate Requirements, Exhibit A and Exhibit B documents, and submits them to the City in writing by August 28, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT. Tracks the City's September 5, 2024 answers and any addenda, and confirms each is incorporated into the Requirements responses, pricing and implementation narrative before the September 17, 2024 submission. Any ambiguity, conflict, discrepancy or omission found in the RFP is raised with the City in writing rather than resolved silently in the proposal.

component_records.title: Project management, methodology and phased plan
component_records.description: Delivers the implementation methodology the City asks for: a sample project plan with phases, tasks and timeline; City and Vendor staffing by role with average hours per month; and the process improvement strategy that treats the project as a move to best practice rather than a like-for-like swap. The plan sequences Financials and HCM module groups across March 2025 to January 2027, with go live for all modules by January 1, 2027 and City approval gates at each phase boundary. A named project manager owns schedule, risk, issue and status reporting to the City throughout.

component_records.title: Requirements response and fit-gap analysis
component_records.description: Completes the City's Requirements document line by line in the unmodified MS Word file, giving every item a rating from the prescribed scale (4, 3, 2, 0 or F) and a comment of no more than 100 words that explains how the item is supported, with no hyperlinks, no cross-references to other line items and no 'standard functionality' shorthand. The same responses feed a fit-gap analysis that identifies modifications, third-party integrations and future-release items, with cost estimates for modifications and month/year for future releases. This is the basis for the functional scope confirmed with the City before configuration begins.

component_records.title: Software configuration and module build
component_records.description: Configures the in-scope Financial modules (General Ledger, Budget, Project and Grant Accounting, Purchasing and Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Capital Assets, Enterprise Cashiering) and HCM modules (Human Resources, Time and Attendance, Payroll) to the City's chart of accounts, budget structure, grant and project accounting rules, procurement and contract workflows, and payroll and time rules. Where a best-of-breed HCM product is proposed, the integration to the ERP is built and tested so HR, time and payroll data flow to Financials. Configuration is delivered in iterative cycles with City review and sign-off per module.

component_records.title: Data conversion by module
component_records.description: Provides a data conversion methodology per module: source data profiling and mapping from the City's legacy environment, cleansing and validation rules, mock conversions and reconciliation reports, and a final cutover conversion with City sign-off on balances and record counts. Conversion scope covers master data (vendors, customers, employees, chart of accounts, assets) and open balances and transactions for each Financial and HCM module in scope.

component_records.title: Integration, reporting and technical architecture
component_records.description: Delivers the integration tools and interfaces needed between ERP modules and any best-of-breed HCM product, plus report development for the City's operational and management reporting needs. Documents the technical architecture options (hosted, on-premises, SaaS), data center locations and redundancy, hardware specifications, mobile options, remote access, integration tools and software update scheduling, and the security overview covering SSO/SAML, multi-factor authentication and breach notification, response and cost. This is the material the City's Technology criterion and security review will assess.

component_records.title: Testing, training and change management
component_records.description: Runs a structured test programme — unit, integration, conference-room pilot, user acceptance and parallel or mock go-live — with documented scripts, defect tracking and City sign-off. Delivers training methodology and tools, role-based end-user and administrator training, and a change management methodology covering stakeholder engagement, communications, readiness assessment and adoption measurement, so the City realises process improvement rather than a system swap. Training materials and documentation are handed over as City property.

component_records.title: Go live, cutover and post go-live support
component_records.description: Executes cutover to go live for all modules by January 1, 2027, with a cutover runbook, go/no-go criteria and hypercare immediately after each go live. Provides ongoing support with stated support hours, guaranteed response times, escalation process, baseline versus premium support levels, backup and disaster recovery services, post go-live tools, and user group and conference access. Support is priced for Years 1-10 alongside license and maintenance.

component_records.title: Pricing on Exhibit A, per deployment option
component_records.description: Completes the Exhibit A Pricing Summary as Section 3 of the response for all Required modules, with software and implementation services costs covering deployment, data conversion, configuration, report development, testing and training, plus integration, travel and other costs. Pricing is comprehensive including all taxes and available discounts, valid 180 days from the response date, sized to 130 named / 85 concurrent Financial users and 400 FTEs / 744 W2s for HCM, and presented on a separate sheet for each deployment option (SaaS and on-premises) with license and maintenance for Years 1-10.

component_records.title: Governance, compliance and contract obligations
component_records.description: Manages the contractual and legal obligations of the bid and the engagement: certification of insurance before any work commences, an underwriter's endorsement with additional insured verbiage from a surety admitted in Washington State, and acknowledgement that all data, materials and documentation prepared for the City belong to the City. Provides the Exhibit B references (three current, two prior customers of similar size and scope, with Washington public-sector preference), the five-year disclosure of terminated contracts or customer legal action, sample contract documents, and a documented list of exceptions to the RFP. Also carries the bidder's own cost of responding and the proposal's compliance with the City's public-records position.

component_records.title: Reference implementations and demo readiness
component_records.description: Presents the Vendor's track record implementing the proposed solution for cities of similar size and scope, drawn from the Exhibit B references and shaped into implementation case summaries. Prepares the delivery team to demonstrate the product on-site against the City's Demo Script, covering best practices and the system's ability to adapt to user preferences, and to show adherence to the script alongside demonstrated fit to the City's functional and technical requirements.

items.text: The RFP is issued by the City of Federal Way, Washington, which incorporated in February 1990 and changed from a council-manager to a mayor-council form of government in November 2010.

The City is a residential and commercial community with an estimated 22,485 people employed within its city limits, and its comprehensive plan calls for a vibrant City Center with mixed-use development and public transportation access.

The City currently runs a legacy environment that it intends to replace with an integrated ERP solution; the RFP's Scope section presents tables describing the current environment and which solutions are in scope, but those tables are not reproduced in the RFP text.
The City's stated business driver is process improvement through new systems and adoption of the selected Vendor's best practices, not a like-for-like system swap.
The City wants a Vendor with a proven track record implementing the proposed solution for cities of similar size and scope of services.
The City is open to best-of-breed Human Capital Management Vendors that can integrate with the selected ERP system, in addition to full-suite ERP Vendors.
The City intends to purchase an integrated ERP solution covering the modules and functionality defined in a separate Requirements document issued with the RFP.

The required Financial modules are General Ledger, Budget, Project and Grant Accounting, Purchasing and Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Capital Assets and Enterprise Cashiering, sized at 130 named users and 85 concurrent users.
The required Human Capital Management modules are Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll, sized at 400 FTEs and 744 W2s.
The City expects a phased implementation, or another approach recommended by the selected Vendor and approved by the City, with implementation running March 2025 through January 2027.

The Vendor must deliver implementation services through go live covering software deployment, data conversion, system configuration, report development, testing and training, plus integration, travel and other costs.

The Vendor must supply an implementation methodology with a sample project plan (phases, tasks, timeline), City and Vendor staffing by role and average hours per month, process improvement strategy, change management methodology, data conversion methodology by module, testing and training methodology and tools, and report development.

The Vendor must provide post go-live support including support hours, guaranteed response time, escalation process, baseline versus premium support levels, backup and disaster recovery services, and user groups and conferences.
Proposals are scored by a City evaluation committee on Software (30 points), Implementation (25 points), Technology (15 points), Vendor (15 points) and Cost Value (15 points).
The Implementation criterion requires Go Live for all modules in scope by January 1, 2027.

Finalists must demonstrate their product on-site following a City-issued Demo Script, and demos are judged on adherence to that script and on demonstrated ability to meet the City's functional and technical requirements.

Every requirement line item must be rated and commented, with ratings of 4 (standard/available), 3 (third-party integrated, application named), 2 (modification, cost estimated), 0 (not available) or F (future release, month and year given); blank responses may cause rejection.
Software missing a significant number of required features and technology preferences may be eliminated from consideration.
Vendor questions are due August 28, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, answers are posted September 5, 2024, and proposals are due September 17, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, with late submissions not considered.

The selection schedule runs finalists selected October 2024, software demos December 2024, due diligence review January 2025, and contract negotiations January 2025 onward, and the City may modify or reschedule these dates.
No contract will be awarded until it is approved by City Council, and the City may award on the initial proposal alone or after demos and negotiations.

Proposals must be a single electronic PDF of no more than 100 pages (sample contracts excluded) emailed to Thuch.Mam@FederalWayWA.gov, plus one completed Requirements document in unmodified MS Word format.

The proposal must follow the prescribed section order — Cover Letter (two pages maximum), Requirements, Pricing, Implementation and Support — and responses that deviate may be classified non-responsive and disqualified, with marketing literature excluded.

Pricing must use the Exhibit A Pricing Summary, be comprehensive including all taxes and discounts, remain valid 180 days from the response date, and include a separate sheet for each deployment option (SaaS or on-premises) with license/maintenance priced for Years 1-10.

The Requirements document must not be reformatted — no changes to format, font, numbering or page breaks — each response is limited to 100 words, and hyperlinks, cross-references to other line items, and comments such as "Standard Functionality" are not acceptable.

The Vendor must describe technical architecture options (hosted, on-premises, SaaS), data center locations and redundancy, hardware specifications, mobile options, remote access, integration tools, and update scheduling, plus a security overview covering SSO/SAML, multi-factor authentication and breach notification, response and cost.

The Vendor must submit three current and two prior customer references on Exhibit B forms, similar in size and scope to the City's project with preference for Washington State public sector clients, and must disclose any contract terminated or legal action with a customer in the past five years.

All data, materials and documentation prepared for the City belong to the City, submissions become public records, and a Vendor cannot mark its entire submittal proprietary — the City makes the sole determination of what is proprietary.

The Requirements document and the Pricing Summary (Exhibit A) and References form (Exhibit B) are separate documents the bidder must obtain and complete, and the current-environment and in-scope solution tables referenced in the Scope section are not included in the RFP text.
Vendor questions are due August 28, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, answers are posted September 5, 2024, and proposals are due September 17, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT.
The City expects implementation to run March 2025 through January 2027 with all modules live by January 1, 2027.
The City's driver is process improvement and adoption of the Vendor's best practices, not a like-for-like system replacement.
The City's functional and technical requirements are held in a separate Requirements document issued with the RFP.
The City is open to best-of-breed HCM vendors that integrate with the selected ERP.
Financials are sized at 130 named users and 85 concurrent users, and HCM at 400 FTEs and 744 W2s.
The City currently runs a legacy environment that the ERP is intended to replace.
The City scores Technology at 15 points and requires architecture, redundancy, mobile, integration and security detail.
The Vendor must deliver testing and training methodology and tools as part of implementation services.
The City requires post go-live support detail including hours, response times, escalation, support tiers, backup and disaster recovery, and user groups.
Pricing must use the Exhibit A template and include a separate sheet for each deployment option.
The City requires an insurance certificate and an underwriter's endorsement with additional insured verbiage from a Washington-admitted surety.
All data, materials and documentation prepared for the City belong to the City, and submissions become public records.
The City wants a Vendor with a proven track record implementing the proposed solution for cities of similar size and scope.
Finalists must demonstrate on-site following a City-issued Demo Script, judged on script adherence and demonstrated fit.
January 1, 2027 is treated as a hard contractual go-live date for all modules, with modules going live in waves before that date rather than all at once.

Insurance is assumed to be quoted at the City's standard public-entity limits (commercial general liability, auto, workers' compensation, professional liability and cyber) with the City named as additional insured, pending the City confirming amounts.
The Requirements document is assumed to match the functional scope described in the RFP's Scope and module sections, and the bid is priced against that scope until the actual document is obtained.
The current-environment and in-scope solution tables are assumed to describe a single legacy system being replaced wholesale, so data conversion is scoped from one source per module.
The Demo Script is assumed to be issued only to finalists, so demo preparation is scheduled after the October 2024 finalist selection rather than during proposal preparation.
The Exhibit A and Exhibit B templates are assumed to be obtainable from the City before the September 17, 2024 deadline, and pricing and references are built directly in those templates.

Requirements document not in hand, so scope and price are estimated blind. The City's functional and technical requirements live in a separate Requirements document that the bid team does not yet hold, and the current-environment and in-scope solution tables are not reproduced in the RFP text. The bid is therefore priced against an assumed scope; if the real document contains modules, interfaces or modifications beyond that assumption, the fixed Exhibit A price and the January 1, 2027 plan both break. The bidder carries the cost of re-rating hundreds of line items if the document arrives late. The RFP states the requirements are in a separate Word document and the scope tables are absent, while the solution explicitly assumes the document matches the RFP's module narrative and prices against that assumption. Pricing a multi-module ERP without the requirement list is expected to produce a gap.

January 1, 2027 go-live treated as hard for all modules. The RFP requires all modules in scope live by January 1, 2027, with implementation running March 2025 to January 2027, but does not settle whether that date is contractual or whether modules may go live in waves. The proposed solution assumes a hard date with wave-based go-lives. If the City instead expects a single simultaneous cutover, or if any wave slips, the bidder faces liquidated exposure or a compressed, more expensive end-game across Financials and HCM. Go live for all modules is a scored Implementation criterion and the date is fixed, but the RFP leaves the phasing question open, so the risk turns on an answer the RFP does not give. A 22-month, eleven-module implementation with data conversion and a possible best-of-breed HCM integration is tight.

Best-of-breed HCM integration adds unquantified scope. The City permits best-of-breed HCM vendors that integrate with the ERP, and the solution builds and tests that integration so HR, time and payroll data flow to Financials. Payroll and time integration is the highest-risk interface in an ERP programme; if the HCM product is third-party, the bidder owns an interface whose effort depends on a product it may not control, and the Exhibit A price must absorb it. The RFP explicitly opens the door to third-party HCM and requires integration capability, and the solution commits to building and testing that interface. The effort depends on which HCM product is proposed and on the City's payroll rules, neither of which the RFP settles.

Insurance limits and additional insured terms unknown at bid time. The RFP requires a certificate of insurance and an underwriter's endorsement naming the City as additional insured from a Washington-admitted surety, but states no coverage types, limits or amounts. The solution assumes standard public-entity limits. If the City's actual limits are higher, or require cyber or professional liability at levels the bidder does not carry, the bidder must buy cover or seek an exception after award, and the cost is not in the price. The requirement is mandatory and the amounts are simply absent from the RFP, so the exposure depends on facts the RFP does not give. Insurance is a pre-work condition, so a shortfall delays mobilisation rather than merely costing money.

Exhibit A and Exhibit B templates not yet obtained. Pricing must be completed on the Exhibit A template as Section 3 and references on Exhibit B forms, but both are separate documents the bidder must obtain. If the templates arrive late or differ from the assumed structure, pricing and reference work is redone close to the September 17, 2024 deadline, and a non-conforming pricing sheet can make the response non-responsive. The solution assumes both templates are obtainable before the deadline, which the RFP does not guarantee. Pricing format is a mandatory submission requirement, so a mismatch is a responsiveness risk, not just rework.

Unreadable page 5 may hide scope or pricing terms. Page 5 of the RFP is dominated by an image block covering 42% of the page and its text could not be parsed. If that page carries scope tables, user counts or pricing instructions, the bid may be built on an incomplete reading of the RFP and miss a mandatory element. The page sits in the early scope section where the current-environment and in-scope solution tables are referenced, and those tables are already noted as not reproduced in the RFP text. The content is unknown, so the impact is plausible rather than certain.

Demo Script withheld until finalist notification. Finalists must demonstrate on-site following a City-issued Demo Script and are judged on script adherence, but the script is only provided with the finalist notification. The solution schedules demo preparation after October 2024 selection. If the script demands scenarios the team has not rehearsed, or the December 2024 demo window is short, the demo score suffers on a criterion the City weights heavily. The script is a referenced document not available at bid time, and the solution's assumption that it arrives only at finalist stage is an inference. Demo performance feeds the Software and Implementation scores, so a weak demo costs ranking.

100-page cap and prescribed format squeeze the response. The proposal must be a single PDF of no more than 100 pages in a prescribed section order, with a two-page cover letter, no marketing literature, and a separate unmodified Word Requirements document. The solution covers eleven components including architecture, security, references, sample contracts and full implementation methodology. Content that does not fit gets cut, and a deviation in order or length can be ruled non-responsive. The page cap is mandatory and the content obligations are extensive, including security, architecture, support and references. The RFP warns that responses deviating from the format may be disqualified, so the constraint bites on both quality and compliance.

Requirements responses constrained to 100 words with no cross-references. Every line item in the Requirements document must be rated on the prescribed scale and explained in 100 words or fewer, with no hyperlinks, no references to other line items and no 'standard functionality' shorthand, in an unmodified Word file. With a large requirement set this is a substantial writing and quality-control effort, and a blank or shorthand response may cause rejection. The RFP states blank responses may cause rejection and explicitly disallows the shorthand vendors normally use. The volume of line items is unknown until the Requirements document is obtained, which makes the effort hard to size.

Pricing must be comprehensive and held for 180 days across two deployment options. Pricing must include all taxes and discounts, cover implementation services through go live, license and maintenance for Years 1-10, and be presented on a separate sheet for each deployment option, valid for 180 days. The solution prices both SaaS and on-premises. If hardware, hosting or third-party costs move during the validity window, or a deployment option is under-scoped, the bidder absorbs the difference on a ten-year commitment. The RFP requires comprehensive pricing on two deployment sheets with a 180-day hold and ten years of maintenance, which locks in cost assumptions well beyond the bid. The solution's own assumption that the scope tables describe a single legacy system also feeds the conversion estimate.

Data conversion scoped from a single assumed legacy source. The solution assumes the current-environment tables describe one legacy system replaced wholesale, so conversion is scoped from one source per module. If the City actually runs several systems, spreadsheets or shadow databases, source profiling, mapping and reconciliation multiply, and the conversion effort priced in Exhibit A is short. The RFP's current-environment tables are not reproduced in the RFP text, so the single-source assumption is unverified. Conversion is a mandatory priced service and a common source of ERP overrun.

Proprietary marking and public-records exposure. All data, materials and documentation prepared for the City belong to the City, submissions become public records, and the City alone decides what is proprietary, while the bidder may not mark the whole submittal proprietary. Pricing detail, methodology and security information therefore become disclosable, and an over-broad confidentiality claim can be rejected or the response treated as non-conforming. The obligation is mandatory and the City holds sole discretion, but the practical impact is limited to disclosure of bid content rather than delivery failure. The solution addresses ownership but not the marking procedure.
